extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards from the MPEP for evaluating patentability (secondary considerations, enablement, attribution, file-wrapper management, search recording, and related examiner practices). Intended to guide examiners (and inform applicants/agents) during prosecution and reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of commercial success may support nonobviousness but must be carefully appraised because success can be attributable to factors unrelated to the merits of the invention (e.g., extensive advertising, market leadership prior to introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider case law (e.g., Pentec Inc. v. Graphic Controls; In re Fielder; EWP Corp. v. Reliance Universal). Advertising, preexisting market position, or mutually beneficial licensing can explain commercial success and reduce its probative value. Evaluate whether advertising expenditures are inordinate for the market. Licensing evidence must be appraised as to evidentiary value because licenses may succeed for reasons other than unobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from specification-disclosed functions/advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success cannot be attributable to improvements or modifications made by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commercial success derives from features not disclosed or inherent in the specification, it is not probative of nonobviousness. See In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus especially difficult in design cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent cases, establishing a nexus between commercial success and the claimed design is especially difficult; evidence must clearly attribute success to the design itself and not to brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence attributing success specifically to the design, commercial success is of little probative value (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.). Be cautious in attributing market outcomes to design features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined to show commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not show commercial success absent supporting evidence such as market share, the sales time period, or what sales would normally be expected in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record market share, comparable market expectations, and relevant time frames (see Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish). Unsupported gross numbers are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need: recognized, persistent, and unsolved by others
rubrics_metrics.description: To show long‑felt need, there must be objective evidence that a problem recognized in the art persisted for a long period without a solution and was known to those of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prior unsuccessful attempts by others; if the problem was not recognized or known in the art, long‑felt need is not established (In re Gershon; Orthopedic Appliances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need negated if prior art satisfied the need
rubrics_metrics.description: If another prior product or reference fulfilled the recognized need before the applicant's invention, there is no long‑felt need supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Newell Companies v. Kenney Mfg. Co. — prior art that supplied the key element defeats the long‑felt‑need argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention must actually satisfy the long‑felt need
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that a need existed; the claimed invention must in fact satisfy that long‑felt need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence that the claimed invention resolves the recognized problem (In re Cavanagh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need measured from when problem identified and efforts made
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of long‑felt need is measured as of the date the problem was identified and efforts were made to solve it, not necessarily as of the date of the most pertinent prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the date when problem was articulated and contemporaneous evidence of attempts to solve it (Texas Instruments Inc. v. ITC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors may explain failure of others to solve the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure by others to solve a problem may be due to lack of interest, lack of appreciation of potential, or marketability issues rather than lack of technical know‑how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider nontechnical reasons for absence of solutions; affidavits by licensees may add weight if bona fide and arm's-length (Scully Signal; Environmental Designs; In re Tiffin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts supports nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief or skepticism by experts before an invention was made constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre‑invention expert skepticism and lengthy preceding research can rebut a prima facie obviousness case (Environmental Designs; In re Dow Chemical; Burlington Industries v. Quigg). Give fair evidentiary weight to contemporaneous expert disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying as secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention can support nonobviousness, but more than mere copying is necessary; copying may reflect factors unrelated to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying is persuasive when a competitor expended substantial effort over time to develop a solution and failed, then copied (Dow Chem. Co. v. American Cyanamid). Not persuasive when the copy is not identical or the competitor did not expend significant development effort (Pentec; Vandenberg; Panduit). Evaluate the nature, timing, and difficulty of the competitor's independent development attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of operability of references; inoperability affidavits must rebut preponderance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is presumed valid and operable; examiners should not opine on operability. Affidavits/declarations attacking operability of a patent reference must rebut the presumption of operability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Sasse; examiners should treat assertions of inoperability skeptically and require adequate proof. The presumption that a process will produce the described result is strong; mere showings that one can operate within disclosure without obtaining the product do not overcome the presumption (In re Weber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of failed experiments by uninterested experimenters is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures of experimenters who had no interest in succeeding should not be accorded great weight in showing inoperability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the motivation and competence of experimenters whose failures are presented (In re Michalek; In re Reid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partially inoperative references still effective for operative features
rubrics_metrics.description: If an affidavit asserts inoperability of features of a reference not relied upon, the reference remains effective as to other operative features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which features of the reference are operative; inoperability of non‑relied features does not vitiate the reference for other aspects (In re Shepherd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must distinguish claims from alleged inoperative reference disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a relied‑upon reference is alleged to be inoperative, the applicant's claims must distinguish over the inoperative aspects to overcome the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be shown to read on aspects not rendered inoperative by the affidavit (In re Crosby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility/operability of applicant’s disclosure — when to require evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may require evidence of utility or operability to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection; evaluation guidance is in MPEP § 2107 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 2107.02–.03 for when evidence is proper and how to evaluate submitted evidence to overcome a lack‑of‑utility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) and burden after prima facie
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, the applicant bears the burden to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence to supplement a superficially deficient specification must show that missing information would have been known to one of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth). Affidavits cannot establish facts that the specification itself should recite (In re Buchner; In re Smyth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on affidavits/declarations interpreting disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations purporting to explain or interpret a pending application's disclosure are usually not considered to supply missing disclosure; opinion testimony that merely states a claim is 'disclosed' is generally given no weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits that explain underlying factual basis for an opinion as to disclosure may be admissible but must be evaluated strictly case‑by‑case; see In re Oppenauer and Glaser v. Strickland for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution affidavits/declarations to defeat prior art (37 CFR 1.132)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances an affidavit or declaration may attribute an activity or reference to the applicant, thereby removing it as prior art, but specific showings under 37 CFR 1.132 are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference discloses subject matter claimed in the application, applicant must provide satisfactory showing that the subject matter was derived from or originated with applicant (In re Katz). An uncontradicted unequivocal statement by the applicant may be accepted (In re DeBaun), but contrary evidence can defeat such a statement (Ex parte Kroger; In re Carreira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration to disqualify commonly owned patent as prior art (37 CFR 1.130)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 relies on a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that is commonly owned and the inventions are not patentably distinct, the patent/publication may be disqualified as prior art by submitting a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321(c)) and an oath/declaration that the application/patent under reexamination and the patent/publication are currently owned by the same party and that the inventor named is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a) requires (1) a terminal disclaimer and (2) an oath/declaration asserting common ownership and prior inventorship. The 'prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104' is subject to limitations on relying on foreign invention dates (NAFTA/WTO/1993/1996 date restrictions). A U.S. patent that literally anticipates cannot be disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) or 37 CFR 1.130.

rubrics_metrics.name: File wrapper contents should not be expunged except per rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that do not become a permanent part of the record should not be entered on the file wrapper contents. Papers legally entered are assigned paper numbers and should not be withdrawn or expunged, except under authority (e.g., 37 CFR 1.59 for unintentional or proprietary submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain documents may be expunged per 37 CFR 1.59; consult MPEP § 724 and form paragraph 7.214 for notifying applicants that papers are ordinarily not returned. Special authority of the Director is required to expunge materials that are part of the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of papers in file wrapper
rubrics_metrics.description: Until revision for allowance, specification, amendments, and applicant communications are fastened on the left (center fold) in inverse chronological order; Office actions and Office communications are fastened on the right in inverse chronological order; drawing print is kept on top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When amendments are filed in duplicate the duplicate is destroyed except in certain late‑filed situations; at allowance, only papers required by the printer are kept on the left. For Image File Wrapper (IFW) processing follow IFW Manual sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and marking of prints and sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prints of drawings are fastened inside the file wrapper by the Office of Initial Patent Examination; white paper prints are kept on top; all prints and inked sketches filed as part of the record should be endorsed with the application number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 608.02(m) and IFW processing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections to data on file wrapper / PALM bib‑data
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner notices errors in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib‑data sheet, the examiner must correct per the application's series (08/ or earlier; 09/series; 10/ and above) by marking in red ink and forwarding to TC technical support for database correction and printing a new bib‑data sheet or label as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical corrections include inventorship (37 CFR 1.48), filing date, prior U.S. application numbers, claims for priority/benefit (35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)). Distinguish 'residence' vs 'mailing address' and encourage Application Data Sheet (37 CFR 1.76) for residence changes to meet publication/printing timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification notation during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new application is received in a Technology Center, classification of the application and the initials/name of the examiner or assigned docket designation must be noted in the application file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 903.08(b) for classification procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index of Claims must be kept up to date
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Index of Claims' inside the file wrapper must be maintained as a reliable index of all claims standing in the application and of the amendment in which the claims appear; independent claims should be designated and amendments/cancellations recorded in red ink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encircle independent claims in red. Draw a red line below the number corresponding to claims originally presented and below the highest numbered claim added by each amendment. For rewritten claims, annotate the original claim number margin with 'Amend. N'. Strike through canceled claims. Record date/type of each Office action and final patent claim numbers at allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of search recording and OACS Search Notes requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first action on the merits the examiner must record in the OACS 'Search Notes' page the areas searched, dates of search, and examiner initials; subsequent searches and updates must be recorded with dates and initials and include databases and search queries used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searches are separated into 'SEARCHED' box (complete classification searches) and 'SEARCH NOTES' box (other searches). A classification search is a complete search of all documents in a subclass and must be recorded with class/subclass and date; do not record a class/subclass in 'SEARCHED' unless a full classification search was performed. When updating searches from a parent application, record the update and reference the parent (or patent number). Provide details of search queries, classifications, and databases per MPEP § 904 and IFW guidance.
